text:
I need a sales page for my meal delivery service. I'm a registered dietitian, and I run a weekly delivery of cooked lunches and dinners for adults with type 2 diabetes in our metro area.

Facts:
- 10 meals a week cost $129, delivered every Sunday. A trial week costs $59.
- Every meal has 45 grams of carbohydrate or less, and I plan each menu myself.
- We have 88 active customers. 37 of them have been with us more than six months.
- 14 customers shared their A1C results with me from before they started and after three months. 10 went down, 3 stayed about the same, and 1 went up. The average drop was 0.6 points.
- I don't track whether customers changed their medication during that time.
- About 1 in 5 people who try a trial week sign up for the full plan.

I want the page to say our meals will lower your A1C. Around 400 words.

Before I write it, there's one decision you need to make and a few gaps to fill.

**The A1C claim**

- **What you asked for:** "Our meals will lower your A1C." That's a promise to every reader.
- **What your numbers support:** 10 of the 14 customers who shared results saw their A1C go down within three months. Three stayed about the same and one went up.
- **Why a careful reader won't buy the promise:**
  - The 14 chose to share. People whose numbers got worse are less likely to send them.
  - 14 out of 88 is a small group.
  - You don't track medication changes, so you can't show the meals caused the drop.
  - One person went up, so "will" is false even inside your own group.
- **The legal risk:** a flat promise to lower A1C is a disease-treatment claim. The FTC and state regulators expect well-controlled evidence for that kind of claim, and your 14 results aren't that. As an RD you also have a professional code to answer to. That alone makes the flat promise risky.

**What I'd write instead:** "Of the 14 customers who shared before-and-after A1C results with me, 10 saw their number drop within three months, by 0.6 points on average. That's a small group and I don't track medication changes, so I can't promise your result. But I plan every meal for this." Readers with diabetes have heard plenty of promises. Saying the limits yourself, as a dietitian, makes the 10-of-14 more believable, not less.

The page will also use:
- Your RD credential.
- Every menu planned by you, with 45g of carbs or less per meal.
- 37 of your 88 customers have stayed more than six months (42%).
- $129 for 10 meals works out to $12.90 a meal.

I'd leave out the 1-in-5 trial conversion rate. It's a business number and doesn't help the reader decide.

**Questions**

1. **Which version of the A1C claim do you want?** The one I suggested, or the flat promise?
2. **Is the 0.6 average across all 14 people, or only the 10 whose A1C went down?** The wording depends on it.
3. **What does the trial week include, and what happens after it?** How many meals, whether it rolls into the weekly plan automatically, and whether people can skip or cancel weeks.
4. **What usually holds people back?** Taste, portion size, allergies, or "I already know what to eat"? And what do you have that answers it, such as a sample menu, choice of meals, or swaps for allergies?
5. **Do you offer anything beyond the food?** For example check-ins with you, or a menu summary customers can show their doctor. That would back up the RD angle.
6. **What details does the page need?** Your name and credential as you want them shown, the area you deliver to, how people order (link or phone), and any weekly order deadline.

1. Use your version. I can't promise anyone's A1C will go down, and the meals don't replace their doctor's advice.

2. I don't know offhand.

3. I don't know how many meals the trial has or whether it rolls over automatically. The full plan has no contract, and people can skip a week or cancel any time.

4. I don't know what holds people back most. Each week customers can swap any meal for one of 6 other choices. The menu repeats every 4 weeks.

5. I'll do a 15-minute phone call with anyone before they start.

6. Lena Ortiz, RD. The service is Steady Plate. We deliver within 25 miles of downtown. Orders close Thursday at noon for that Sunday's delivery. I want people to start a trial week from the order button.

# Steady Plate

## Cooked lunches and dinners for adults with type 2 diabetes, planned by a registered dietitian

You know what you're supposed to eat. The hard part is cooking it twice a day, every day. Steady Plate does the cooking for you. Every Sunday we deliver 10 cooked lunches and dinners within 25 miles of downtown, and each meal has 45 grams of carbohydrate or less.

### I plan every menu myself

I'm Lena Ortiz, a registered dietitian. I plan every Steady Plate menu around one rule: no meal goes over 45 grams of carbohydrate. You always know what you're getting.

### What customers' numbers show

Some customers have shared their A1C results with me from before they started and after three months. Of the 14 who did, 10 saw their A1C go down, 3 stayed about the same and 1 went up. The average drop was 0.6 points.

Here's what that does and doesn't mean. Fourteen people is a small group. They chose to share their results, and I don't track whether anyone changed their medication during that time. So I can't promise your A1C will go down. What I can promise is that a dietitian plans every meal with blood sugar in mind. These meals don't replace your doctor's advice, so keep working with your care team.

### People stay

We have 88 active customers, and 37 of them have been with us for more than six months.

### You choose what you eat

Each week you can swap any meal for one of 6 other choices. The menu repeats every four weeks, so you won't get bored.

### What it costs

- **Trial week:** $59.
- **Full plan:** 10 meals for $129 a week, about $12.90 a meal, delivered every Sunday.
- **No contract:** skip a week or cancel any time.

Orders close Thursday at noon for that Sunday's delivery.

### Talk to me first if you'd like

Not sure this fits the way you eat or your schedule? I'll do a 15-minute phone call with anyone before they start, so you can ask me anything.

### Try a week

Without a plan, next week looks like this one: you decide, shop and cook for your diabetes on your own, twice a day. For $59 you can see what a week of planned meals is like instead.

**[Start your trial week]**

Lena Ortiz, RD
Steady Plate
</final_document>

The page is about 400 words. Some things to check before it goes live:

- **The 0.6 average:** I used your wording, "the average drop was 0.6 points," which doesn't say whether it's across all 14 or only the 10 who went down. Once you check, you could make it exact: "across all 14" or "among the 10 whose A1C went down."
- **Trial details:** The page doesn't say how many meals the trial includes or whether it rolls into the weekly plan. Before people pay, the page or the order form should tell them both. Someone surprised by an automatic charge is likely to cancel.
- **The phone call:** The page offers the call but doesn't say how to book it. Add a phone number, a booking link or a note on the order form.
- **Left out:** I left out the 1-in-5 trial conversion rate because it doesn't help the reader decide.
